role: Marketing specialist at a multinational consumer-goods brand
headline: A marketing specialist at a multinational FMCG company in Shanghai, two years out of a big ad agency and into a client-side job, carrying the launch of a new sugar-free tea and its Xiaohongshu and Douyin spend, checking reach and conversion before anything else each morning
unit: The beverages division of a multinational consumer-goods company in Jing'an, Shanghai
level: You can write a brief on your own, sign up influencers and watch the ad dashboards, and you know how seeding works on Xiaohongshu. Return on spend and budget splits still need your manager's sign-off, and your English presentations still stumble
intro: You spent a year as an account executive at an ad agency, rewriting hundreds of decks for clients, and last year you crossed over to the client side. This year the company is launching a sugar-free tea across East China, and your manager has handed you the paid campaigns on Xiaohongshu and Douyin. The KPIs sit on the first line of the weekly report: reach, engagement, conversion. As of today, every number on the dashboard is yours to explain.
salary_note: Estimate: a marketing specialist at a multinational FMCG company in Shanghai earns a little over ¥10,000 a month, plus a year-end bonus and an extra housing fund contribution, 40-50% above the national figure. But multinationals have been shrinking their China teams for years, and raises get smaller every year.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Triggering a level-three response when a PR crisis breaks, and drafting the first statement

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Building a campus launch plan for a new product, with a one-page proposal

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 275 related job listings nationwide, 41 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: You leave the shared flat in Pudong and squeeze onto Line 2 to Jing'an Temple. On the train you scroll through the twenty sponsored posts that went out last night. One has lost most of its engagement, and somebody in the comments has written: “this looks like an ad.”

Before the morning meeting you pull the numbers: reach, clicks, cost per engagement, store visits, a spreadsheet blotched red and green. Your manager only reads the last column, and asks why conversion is down on last week.

A launch-schedule meeting with the agency. The account executive across the table was your peer a year ago; now you sit on the other side, and when he says “this budget is going to be tricky,” you know exactly what he's thinking.

Legal sends back three influencer scripts. “Guilt-free” is out. “The most refreshing” is out. Even “first sip” needs thought. You fix them line by line, send them back to the influencers line by line, and keep smiling.

An Asia-Pacific video call, presenting the Shanghai pilot numbers in English. You rehearsed three times. Someone in Singapore cuts in with a question, you freeze for five seconds, and your manager picks it up for you.

You check the shelves at two convenience stores downstairs. The new tea is on the second shelf of the cooler, elbowed to the edge by a domestic brand. You take a photo, buy a bottle of your own, and drink it standing at the door.
Home at last, and the influencer says the video will be a day late. In the group chat you juggle the editor, the platform and legal while the takeout goes cold on the table.
One last look at the live numbers before bed, and a post has suddenly started climbing. You screenshot it to your manager, get no reply, and fall asleep like that.

ladder.title: Marketing Specialist
ladder.focus: Produce social media content, keep campaign schedules on track, sign up influencers and get materials delivered. You move up on flawless delivery, a sharp ear for copy and projects that run without a single slip.

ladder.title: Senior Marketing Specialist
ladder.focus: Own a channel on your own, such as Xiaohongshu or in-feed ads, or plan a mid-sized integrated campaign. You move up on a benchmark viral case and a clear review of return on ad spend.

ladder.title: Marketing Manager
ladder.focus: Run quarterly and annual integrated marketing plans, split budgets, set the channel mix and train the team. You move up on growth in leads or sales at scale and influence across departments.

ladder.title: Senior Marketing Manager
ladder.focus: Run full-funnel marketing across several business lines or a flagship product, break the brand out into wider conversation, and join up public channels with the brand's own. You move up on tight control of budgets in the tens of millions and on opening a second growth curve.

ladder.title: Marketing Director
ladder.focus: Set company-wide brand strategy, the line on reputation, and the annual growth engine; you answer directly for brand equity and overall return. You report to the CEO or a business vice president.

ai_tasks.name: Building a campus launch plan for a new product, with a one-page proposal
ai_tasks.how: AI can gather campus consumer insights, generate several strategies and draft budgets, and lay out the one-pager. A person has to make the trade-offs within a ¥500,000 budget and a three-month window, set the stop-loss line, and answer for the final plan.

ai_tasks.name: Writing the launch promotion plan and the stop-loss contingency
ai_tasks.how: AI drafts the first version of both and quickly tests different channel mixes. A person judges what the East China campus market is really like, decides what to cut and what to keep, and answers for the result.

ai_tasks.name: Quality-checking the first round of micro-influencer posts in launch week and closing the feedback loop
ai_tasks.how: AI scans fifty micro-influencers' posts in bulk, flags off-brief ideas, likely banned wording and muddled messaging, and drafts the feedback. A person reviews the borderline cases, talks the influencers into the changes, and handles the relationship and the tone.

ai_tasks.name: Pulling a micro-influencer post that may break advertising rules
ai_tasks.how: AI watches for banned claims, raises the alarm and drafts corrected wording. A person confirms within two hours whether it is a violation, gets the influencer and the platform to take it down, traces where it came from, and answers for the compliance fallout.

ai_tasks.name: Recalibrating the competitor price-tracking scraper and filing the report before quarter end
ai_tasks.how: AI and scripts can fix the scraper logic, clean the data, compare prices and draft the brief. A person only spot-checks for gaps and consistent definitions, and gives the conclusions a final check.

ai_tasks.name: Triggering a level-three response when a PR crisis breaks, and drafting the first statement
ai_tasks.how: AI can track how the story is spreading, lay out the facts and draft a first statement. But triggering the response, coordinating with legal and PR for a joint sign-off, and deciding what to say in public all take a person's judgment and a person's responsibility.

ai_tasks.name: Switching in-feed ad creatives between A/B groups before the lunchtime traffic peak
ai_tasks.how: AI picks the best creative combination from live data and switches it in automatically. A person sets the rules and the red lines, and spot-checks unusual swings and creative compliance.

ai_tasks.name: Producing the first Singles' Day results report within thirty minutes of midnight and briefing every department
ai_tasks.how: AI pulls together sales, stock-out warnings and livestream anomalies in real time and writes a structured report. A person works out what lies behind the numbers, decides what to stress to the CEO, sales and supply chain, and gets everyone moving.

events.e_viral: The “third coffee of overtime” post you wrote the brief for went viral, past fifty thousand likes in a night. Your manager put the screenshot on the first slide at the weekly meeting. He didn't say who wrote it, but everyone knew.
events.e_limit: A batch of influencer posts got throttled by the platform for “excessive marketing,” and reach fell by seventy percent. You spent a night going through the platform rules before you found it: twenty people had used the same line.
events.e_mentor: Your manager walked you through last quarter's ad spend and told you to stop looking at reach and look at how many bottles each yuan finally bought. That day, for the first time, the numbers in the spreadsheet felt alive.
events.e_shelf: Home in Anhui for the New Year, you found the tea in the cooler of a county-town supermarket, wearing the price sticker you'd revised a dozen times. You sent your mother a photo: I made this. She replied with three thumbs up.
events.e_double11: Midnight on Singles' Day, you and the e-commerce team kept watch over the big screen in a meeting room, a new results report every hour. It broke up at four in the morning, and you were somewhere past a hundred in the ride-hailing queue.
events.e_love: At a friend's board-game night you met someone who designs video games. You both answered messages in the middle of the night. After a while you didn't need to, because you'd moved in together.
events.e_village: You went with the sales team to small shops in the townships of northern Jiangsu. One owner said young people pick drinks by whichever bottle stands out in the cooler, and never look at ads. Back in the office you rewrote half of the second-half materials plan.
events.e_budget_cut: Headquarters redid the annual budget and cut China marketing by a fifth. One of your three projects went, and you had to apologize, one by one, to the influencers you'd spent two months lining up.
events.e_kol_flip: A top influencer you'd signed for six months was caught in a scandal, and overnight the comments filled with abuse. You took down every joint post that night and rewrote the incident summary for headquarters seven times.
events.e_wedding: You had a small wedding. You designed the invitations yourself, on a pitch-deck template. The gift money just about covered the banquet.
events.e_ai_creative: The company plugged in AI for images and copy, and one afternoon could produce two hundred versions of creative. You went from writing copy to choosing it and fixing it, and checking every line for banned words.
events.e_crisis: Someone posted that they'd found something in your tea, and within half a day it had ten thousand shares. You worked three days straight with PR and legal, weighing the statement word by word. It turned out to be fake. You sat at your desk for a long time before you went home.
events.e_ai_ab: The ad platform started swapping creatives on its own, and before the lunchtime peak it had pulled the weak versions before you got to them. Your job became setting rules, watching for anomalies, and explaining to your boss why the machine chose what it chose.
events.e_insomnia: After several big sales events in a row, you woke at two in the morning and reached for your phone to check the numbers. The checkup said thyroid nodules and mild fatty liver. You put the report at the bottom of a drawer.
events.e_award: The launch you ran was named the region's case of the year. You flew to Singapore to collect it and spoke for five minutes on stage in English without stumbling once.
events.e_house: You bought a two-bedroom flat in an old estate outside the Outer Ring Road, and the down payment emptied both families' savings. The commute grew by twenty minutes, and you filled them with podcasts.
events.e_baby: The baby arrived. When you came back from leave, your desk had been moved by the door. For the first week of meetings, you checked every number in your notebook before you said it aloud.
events.e_ai_report: The Singles' Day results report is now written by AI and lands in the group chat at 12:30 sharp. Your job is to read it: where stock is running out, which livestream has dropped, who needs to hear it, and what to say first.
events.e_layoff: A restructuring of the China business, and the team next door was let go, all of them, with the legal severance plus a month. The next day their desks were empty. The potted plants were still there.
events.e_mentee: The graduate you'd been training wrote her first viral post and forwarded you the screenshot with a string of exclamation marks. You remembered your own first one, when no one knew who'd written it.
events.e_guochao: A dozen domestic tea brands appeared in a year, and prices fell to ¥3.90 a bottle. Headquarters sent someone to ask why the China team couldn't hold the line. You'd prepared a one-page answer. No one turned to that page.
events.e_parent: A call from home: your father had a heart stent put in. You ran two video meetings from the hospital corridor, and a nurse came over to ask you to keep your voice down.
events.e_age35: Scrolling the job apps, you saw half the roles at your level say “under 35.” You deleted your birth year from your résumé, then put it back.

c_cert.title: Get certified in paid media and take over the ad platforms
c_cert.situation: The department wants one person to run the Ocean Engine and Xiaohongshu ad accounts full-time, and that person first has to pass the platforms' certification, which means evening and weekend courses. But you prefer making content. That's why you went into this line of work.

options.label: Get certified, take the media
options.result: You got through the courses in two weekends and passed. From then on your screen had a row of bidding curves, and the day your cost per thousand impressions came down, your manager called you out by name in the group chat.

options.label: Stay on content
options.result: The certification went to a colleague. You kept writing briefs and picking influencers, and the hits came more often, but at every review, he was the one who talked about return on spend.

c_senior.title: Go for Senior Marketing Specialist and take a whole channel
c_senior.situation: Your manager asks if you want all of Xiaohongshu, running the launch of a new flavor in the second half on your own. That's the work of a Senior Marketing Specialist, and if it fails, it fails under your name.

options.label: Take it, run it yourself
options.result: For the first time you signed your own budget and set your own stop-loss line. You lost four pounds in launch week. At the review the total beat the forecast, and one channel lost everything.

options.label: Follow for another year
options.result: You worked under your manager for another year without a single mistake, and without anyone remembering what you did.

c_bigtech.title: Jump to a tech giant to work on growth
c_bigtech.situation: A headhunter calls: a user-growth role at a big internet company in Hangzhou, pay forty percent higher, stock options on top. They work six days every other week, and old colleagues say half the people who go in are out within two years.

options.label: Go to Hangzhou
options.result: You learned to read retention curves and funnels, and your weekly report grew from one page to twenty. The pay went up, the weekends disappeared, and now and then you missed those convenience-store coolers.

options.label: Stay in consumer goods
options.result: You stayed, still doing sums between coolers and shelves. The bonus isn't much, but most days you're out of the office by eight.

c_ai_flow.title: Learn the AI content pipeline or not
c_ai_flow.situation: The company wants an AI content line: AI writes the first draft, makes the images and checks for banned words, and people only review and fix. Headquarters wants someone from marketing to design it, which means learning prompts and building workflows while keeping your projects going.

options.label: Sign up, build the pipeline
options.result: You took the team from forty pieces of creative a month to four hundred, and became the first person asked, “So how many people do we still need?”

options.label: Stay out, guard the creative judgment
options.result: You still edit every draft and talk to every influencer yourself. The AI drafts multiply and fewer people can tell which one will cause trouble, so people start bringing their drafts to you.

c_guochao.title: Join a fast-rising domestic brand
c_guochao.situation: A domestic tea brand that just raised money wants you to lead a team of five, reporting straight to the founder. The pay is only ten percent more, but every call is yours. A friend warns you that companies like that may not be around in three years.

options.label: Join the domestic brand
options.result: For the first time you led people and spent a budget you set yourself. One quarter you beat your old employer on Douyin, and you got drunk at the celebration.

options.label: Stay at the multinational
options.result: You stayed inside the system: slow processes, endless reporting, and a salary that lands on time every month. A year later, that domestic brand laid off half its staff.

c_manager.title: Become a Marketing Manager, or stay the specialist
c_manager.situation: The manager's job is open, and the director asks if you want the team: budgets, people, and the fights with sales. The other path is to stay hands-on and be the person in the company who knows content and media best.

options.label: Take the manager's job
options.result: You started writing annual budgets and scoring your reports' performance, with meetings from morning to night. The last time you wrote copy yourself was six months ago.

options.label: Stay hands-on
options.result: You turned it down, and the director was a little surprised. You're still the one checking numbers at midnight, only now your weekly report goes straight to the director.

c_layoff.title: China layoffs: take the payout and go?
c_layoff.situation: The company announces another round of cuts in China, with three extra months' pay for anyone who leaves voluntarily. You run the numbers on the mortgage, and think of the thing you've wanted to try for years: a small studio making content for small brands.

options.label: Take the money, open the studio
options.result: You took the payout and rented a small office with a former colleague from the agency.
options.end: You opened a content studio on the second floor of an old villa, taking launch projects from young brands. There aren't many clients, and you went out and won every one of them yourself.

options.label: Stay
options.result: You stayed. The team lost three people and none of the work. You learned to write a few lines less in your weekly report.

c_director.title: Run for Marketing Director
c_director.situation: The director is moving back to regional headquarters, and the job is open. Candidates must present a three-year brand strategy in English to the global vice president, and two outside candidates are also in the running.

options.label: Put your name in
options.result: You spent a month on a forty-page plan. When you finished, the vice president's first question landed on the very page you were least sure of.

options.label: Step aside for the outsiders
options.result: The new director came from another consumer-goods company. In his first week he took you for coffee and asked you what was really going on in this market.

c_teach.title: Go back to your old university to teach marketing
c_teach.situation: Your old business school wants a full-time lecturer with real experience to teach integrated marketing and digital media. Half the income, summer and winter breaks, and no more live numbers in the middle of the night.

options.label: Go and teach
options.result: You turned these years of cases into lecture slides.
options.end: You stand at the lectern telling the story of how that sugar-free tea was launched. When you get to the second shelf of the convenience-store cooler, a student at the back raises a hand and asks whether you regretted it.

options.label: Stay on the brand side
options.result: You said no, there was another new product to launch. That winter you made it through one more Singles' Day.

endings.retire: On the last day you hand your laptop to IT and leave your badge at reception. At the convenience store downstairs you buy a bottle of that tea. The recipe has changed three times and the packaging five, but the cooler is the same cooler. You twist it open, take a sip, and ride the metro home without looking at the numbers on your phone again.
endings.burnout: After the fourth meeting that day you sat in the restroom for twenty minutes and your heart would not slow down. The doctor told you to stop for a while. You handed in your notice and wrote thirty pages of handover notes. It was four in the afternoon when you walked out of the tower, and you hadn't seen the sun at that hour in a long time.

past: You went to high school in a small city in Anhui, and your favorite thing was writing the headlines for your class's chalkboard newspaper. Your Chinese teacher said your writing had a feel for the internet. You didn't know then that it would become a job.

You got into a finance and economics university in Shanghai through the gaokao (college entrance exam). Your first choice was finance; you were reassigned to marketing. Your mother called to ask if that meant selling things. You said more or less.
In your third year you interned at a big international ad agency, revising slide decks for clients until the small hours, and learned that one slogan can be rewritten a hundred times.
You applied to five consumer-goods companies' management-trainee programs and got as far as one final interview. They asked, “How would you prove you can drive growth?” You had no answer.
After graduating you stayed at the agency as an account executive and spent a whole year running Xiaohongshu for a drinks brand. You built an influencer list more complete than the client's own.
The client's marketing manager liked your list and your temperament, and hired you away. On your first day you were handed a badge printed with your English name.

late.pension_note: Estimate: Shanghai's basic pension for company employees is based on a fairly high contribution base, and with the multinational's company annuity, your pension comes to about forty percent of your final monthly pay.
scenes: For the first few months of retirement you still opened your phone at eight to check the numbers, and only after a while remembered there were none to check. You muted the work groups one by one.

A former report of yours became a director and asked you to give a talk to the team. You told them how that tea squeezed its way onto the second shelf. The young people listened closely, and someone wrote down the parts AI can't do.
You started a reading group on your estate and made the poster yourself. A dozen older neighbors came, and you sat in the middle watching them photograph the poster on their phones.
You noticed the supermarket had stopped stocking that tea, and its shelf had gone to a brand you'd never heard of. You picked one up, read the ingredients, and put it in your basket.
For the first month after you quit you did nothing at all, just a walk around the park every day, watching the old people do tai chi. The quiet of your phone felt strange.
You took on bits of copywriting, working from home and paid by the piece. Halfway through you'd stop and wonder whether this one would be throttled, then laugh at yourself.
Fewer arrows on the checkup report. You learned to cook, and video-called your parents twice a week, talking mostly about the price of vegetables.
In the first year away from the brand side you still lingered in front of convenience-store coolers, noting whose displays were good.
The new life was neither good nor bad. One year it nearly went under, and an old client's new product pulled it back.

The people you trained and taught are scattered across brands now, and some have become directors. When they send you their new products, you can always spot at a glance the line on the pack that legal won't pass.

Later, the copy, the images and the ad buying all went to machines, and the marketing department kept shrinking. But whenever something went wrong, someone still had to stand up and decide what to say and what not to.
A child in the family asked what you used to do. You said you made people know about a bottle of tea. They didn't quite get it, so you dug an old bottle out of a cupboard, its label faded.

closing.retire: Many years later, on a summer evening, you sit outside a corner convenience store and watch a few young people on their way home from work stand at the cooler, unable to decide. You say nothing. You just watch to see which bottle they take.
closing.burnout: Many years later you grow a row of mint and lemongrass on the balcony, and in summer you make a pot of cold tea, no sugar. You take a photo of it, add no caption, and never post it.
closing.end: Many years later you come across your first marketing assignment from university, its title trying far too hard. You smile, and with a red pen cut it in half.

stages: Your day is a schedule and an influencer group chat. Mornings you write briefs and check creative; afternoons you watch the numbers and adjust bids in the Xiaohongshu and Ocean Engine dashboards; evenings you chase influencers for their posts on WeChat Work. Legal, design, the agency's account executives: you chase them all, politely. You execute; your manager decides.

You run a whole channel now. Each quarter you write the media strategy and split the budget yourself, and schedule dozens of influencers in a Feishu spreadsheet. At reviews you present the return on spend, and your manager asks a question or two at the end. New specialists ask you for templates, and the agency calls you directly instead of going to your manager first.

You've gone from writing plans to signing them off. Every day you read your team's briefs and media reports and write in the margins; you fight sales over channel fees and settle quarterly budgets with headquarters, slicing a year of marketing into slide after slide. You have four people under you, and the thing you say most is: check this number again.

You run the full funnel for a flagship product. Half your week is in meeting rooms: stocking up for sales events with e-commerce, sales and supply chain, planning share of voice with PR, settling budgets in the tens of millions with finance. You sign more and write less, and when agencies pitch, you sit on the judging panel.

You report to the China general manager, and the whole brand is yours. Once a year you build a three-year strategy and present it in English on the global call; each month you read the P&L and decide which brands get more money and which get cut; when a crisis breaks, the final signature is yours. You have more than a dozen people, and you remember each one's first viral post.
work: Design sends twelve versions of the new product's hero image. In WeChat Work you mark up each one: brighten the bottle, move the price sticker to bottom left. Version thirteen finally passes.
In the Xiaohongshu influencer marketplace you send collaboration invites to thirty mid-tier creators, filtered by audience profile over an afternoon. Eleven write back.
The agency's account executive sends the video script at one in the morning. You leave twenty comments in the shared doc, the last one reading: say the brand name more slowly.
In Ocean Engine you set up six campaigns for the new flavor, crossing audiences with creatives. Three days later you shut four down; the other two convert ten percent cheaper than forecast.
In a Feishu spreadsheet you lay out the posting schedule for eighty influencers over the second half, color-coded. Your manager glances at it once and says: go with this.
A regional sales manager calls to complain the materials never arrived. You pull up the tracking numbers and walk him through them one by one, until you find the warehouse got the address wrong.
A report hands in a five-page launch brief. You cross out three paragraphs on the first page and write beside them: in one sentence, who do we want to buy this.
You and the sales director argue in a meeting room for an hour over two million yuan in channel fees. In the end you each give a little, and you sign the minutes.
At mid-year reviews you spend forty minutes going through the appraisal form with a specialist who has missed target two quarters running, and settle on a three-month improvement plan.
Three agencies pitch. You sit on the panel all day, and on the score sheet give the cheapest one the highest mark, with half a page of reasons.
A week before the big sale you go line by line through the stock plan with the supply-chain manager, and cut the stock of two flavors by thirty percent each.
The PR manager brings a media plan. In the budget sheet you move half the influencer money to pop-up events, saying this year people need something they can touch.
On the global video call you present next year's China brand strategy in English. On slide twelve, the vice president in the US stops you with a question about a price tier.
The finance director sends the quarterly P&L. You read it for twenty minutes in a meeting room and decide to shut down a sub-brand that has run for five years.
A new management trainee rotates through. You spend an hour telling them about your first viral post, then send them to stand in front of a convenience-store cooler for an afternoon.
